newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany rejects Amnesty criticism of police abuse.
newsitem.headline: Germany rejects Amnesty criticism of police abuse.

text.p: Germany rejected accusations by Amnesty International on Thursday that its police had systematically ill-treated foreigners in the last two years and that much of the alleged abuse was racially motivated.
"German police are not xenophobic," said Interior Minister Manfred Kanther and Armin Jaeger, head of the interior ministers' conference of the federal states, in a statement.
"Those like Amnesty International who talk about 'models of maltreatment' in the police or say complaints are not carefully followed up is avoiding speaking the truth," they said.

The London-based human rights organisation, which first criticised German police behaviour in 1995, made the claims in a report which examined a variety of evidence from German inquiries into allegations of police violence.

"These -- together with the conclusions of the (U.N.'s) human rights committee which examined Germany's human rights record in November 1996 -- support Amnesty International's view that cases of alleged police ill-treatment are not isolated incidents but amount to a clear pattern of abuse," it said.

Amnesty said many people accused the police of using excessive or unwarranted force in restraining or arresting people and of deliberately subjecting detainees to cruel, inhuman treatment or punishment.

"As in previous years, the vast majority of the victims are foregn nationals, including asylum-seekers or members of ethnic minorities. In many instances, the alleged ill-treatment appears to have been racially-motivated," it said.

"Medical evidence shows the injuries suffered by detainees -- mainly bruising and abrasions, and in some cases broken bones -- to be consistent with their allegations of having been punched, kicked or struck with a police baton."

Amnesty said the German authorities had investigated all the cases reported to the human rights group but said in many cases the inquiries had not been carried out thoroughly, impartially or promptly.

"Many of the officers allegedly responsible have therefore escaped prosecution. Few, if any, have faced disciplinary sanctions, and none of the foreign or ethnic minority complainants have been compensated for the injuries they have suffered," it added.
Amnesty called on the German government to set up additional mechanisms to investigate allegations of police ill-treatment.

"We recognise that the police have a difficult and often dangerous job...However, the authorities have a responsibility to ensure that deliberate ill-treatment, or excessive force amounting to ill-treatment, will not be tolerated under any circumstances," it said.

But Kanther and Jaeger said Germany dealt objectively with individual incidents of incorrect procedure by police officers and independent state prosecutors and courts followed them up with the necessary legal measures.
"There is still no doubt that German police fulfil their difficult tasks true to the law," they said.
